summary: This proposed standard defines MIB objects for managing the IP Network Control Protocol on interfaces that use the Point-to-Point Protocol family.

eli5.summary: PPP connects two computers over a line. This paper lists what a network manager can check about the part that carries Internet traffic on that line.

questions: snmp objects for ppp ip control protocol
what is the ppp ip mib
which snmp objects manage ppp ip
subtitle: The SNMP objects a network manager can read and set to watch and control IP running over a PPP link.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to see and control how IP is running over Point-to-Point Protocol links, but PPP is a large family of protocols and each part needs its own management objects.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the PPP-IP-NCP-MIB module, a small set of SNMP objects in two tables indexed by ifIndex: one for status of the IP Control Protocol and one for configuration.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted or updated, and it covers only the IP group of the wider PPP MIB.

facts.label: Group status
facts.value: Mandatory for PPP that supports IP

today: RFC 1473 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers only the PPP IP Group of the wider PPP MIB.

sections.title: The Management Framework It Plugs Into
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework has three components. SMI (RFC 1155, with the more concise description style in RFC 1212) describes how objects are named and described. MIB-II (RFC 1213) is the core set of managed objects. SNMP (RFC 1157) is the protocol used to reach those objects over the network.

Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER and is written in the subset of ASN.1 that the SMI allows. This memo adds new objects to that store.
sections.eli5: Think of a big instruction panel for network gear. There are rules for how each dial is named, a basic set of dials every device has, and a way to read them from far away. This memo adds some new dials.

sections.title: What PPP Looks Like and What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
The memo explains that PPP is not one protocol but a large family, and splits it into three rough categories. Control Protocols (LCP, PAP, LQR and CHAP) control PPP itself. Network Protocols carry the traffic of a specific higher-layer protocol over the PPP interface. Network Control Protocols (NCPs) control the Network Protocols, usually one NCP for each, so IP has the IP Control Protocol.

This document manages only one of these: the IP Network Control Protocol. The wider PPP MIB is arranged in groups (Link, LQR, LQR Extensions, IP, Bridge and Security), and this memo specifies just the PPP IP Group. A group is the basic unit of conformance: if its semantics apply to an implementation, all objects in it must be implemented. The IP Group is mandatory for every PPP implementation that supports IP over PPP.
sections.eli5: PPP is a toolbox with many tools: some run the line, some carry the mail, and some set up each kind of mail. This memo only covers the tool that sets up Internet mail.

sections.title: Keeping the MIB Small
sections.content:
The author kept the MIB deliberately simple, in line with IAB directives and good engineering practice. Four criteria decided which objects got in.

  • Objects must be essential for fault or configuration management. Objects whose only purpose is debugging implementations are excluded.
  • Evidence of current use or usefulness is considered.
  • The total number of objects is limited.
  • Objects that can simply be derived from others, in this or other MIBs, are left out.
sections.eli5: The authors only added a dial if someone really needed it. No dials just for the repair crew, and no dials that repeat what another dial already shows.

sections.title: The Status Table
sections.content:
The module is called PPP-IP-NCP-MIB. It hangs pppIp under the ppp object imported from PPP-LCP-MIB, and it holds two tables, each with one row per interface, indexed by ifIndex from MIB-II.

The first, pppIpTable, is read-only status for the IP Control Protocol on a link. pppIpOperStatus is opened(1) or not-opened(2), and says whether the IP network protocol's finite state machine has reached the Opened state. Four more objects report what option negotiation produced: pppIpLocalToRemoteCompressionProtocol and pppIpRemoteToLocalCompressionProtocol (each none(1) or vj-tcp(2)) and pppIpRemoteMaxSlotId and pppIpLocalMaxSlotId (each 0 to 255, and 0 when vj-tcp header compression is not in use).

Those four option objects are meaningful only after negotiation finishes, which means pppIpOperStatus is opened. Otherwise their contents are undefined, and what an implementation returns is up to it.
sections.eli5: The first table is a set of gauges. One says whether the Internet part of the line is up, and the others say what speed-up tricks the two ends agreed on.

sections.title: The Configuration Table
sections.content:
The second table, pppIpConfigTable, is kept separate so that its variables can be placed in a separate MIB view. It has two read-write objects.

pppIpConfigAdminStatus is open(1) or close(2). Setting it to open injects an administrative open event into the IP network protocol's finite state machine, and setting it to close injects an administrative close event.

pppIpConfigCompression is none(1) or vj-tcp(2) and defaults to none. With none, the local node will not try to negotiate any IP compression option. Otherwise it will try to negotiate the chosen mode. A change takes effect when the link is next restarted. The object cites the Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression section of RFC 1332.
sections.eli5: The second table has switches. One switch turns the Internet part of the line on or off. The other asks the two ends to try a speed-up trick the next time the line restarts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The PPP MIB lets an operator configure and control PPP links, including the authentication protocols, and the memo says this is a security risk. It names three ways to address it.

  • Variables with significant risk go into separate, optional MIB groups, so an implementor may choose not to implement them.
  • An implementor may make risky variables read-only. This still leaves a risk, because authentication variables may be easily read, so it is not recommended.
  • With SNMPv2, the operator can put the variables into MIB views protected by authentication and privacy protocols, or make the views inaccessible to every party. Security-related variables sit in separate tables to make the view subtree easy to identify.
sections.eli5: Because these switches can change how the line works, the memo says to lock the risky ones in a cabinet, make them look-only, or let only people with the right key reach them.
